title: Module 4 · IV to PO Conversions
intro: When to switch, the 1:1 drugs, the drugs that need a dose change, when not to switch, chelation, feeding tubes, linezolid interactions and how to run the daily IV to PO round.

cases.title: Is this patient ready for oral?
cases.stem: Day 3 of IV levofloxacin for community acquired pneumonia. Afebrile 36 hours, heart rate 84, BP 128/76, eating breakfast, WBC down from 16 to 9.

steps.q: Which findings support switching to oral?

options.t: Working gut: eating and taking other oral meds
options.why: No vomiting, no ileus, no malabsorption.
Afebrile, normal vitals, falling WBC.

options.t: An oral drug with good absorption exists for this infection
options.why: Levofloxacin is about 99% absorbed.
Preference matters, but the clinical criteria decide.

steps.q: What is the oral levofloxacin dose if she is on 750 mg IV daily?

options.why: Levofloxacin oral absorption is nearly complete.
No dose increase needed.

steps.q: Why switch at all?

options.t: Fewer line infections and phlebitis, earlier discharge, lower cost, less nursing time
options.why: IV to PO is one of the simplest high value interventions a pharmacist makes every day.
Not better; equivalent when absorption is good.

cases.pearl: **Gut works, patient improving, good oral drug: switch.**

sources.t: Cyriac JM, James E. Switch over from intravenous to oral therapy: a concise overview. J Pharmacol Pharmacother 2014;5:83-87

cases.title: The 1:1 drugs
cases.stem: You are learning the drugs that convert at the same dose because oral absorption is excellent.

steps.q: Which convert 1:1 IV to PO?

options.why: Nearly complete absorption.
About 100% absorbed.
Nearly complete absorption.
Over 90% absorbed.
Oral vancomycin is not absorbed; it only treats C. difficile in the gut.

steps.q: Which non antibiotics also convert about 1:1?

options.why: IV and oral are interchangeable at the same dose.
IV acetaminophen is mainly for patients who cannot swallow.
Common automatic switch.
Oral furosemide is only about half absorbed and highly variable.

cases.pearl: **1:1 club: levo, moxi, linezolid, metronidazole, fluconazole, levetiracetam, APAP, pantoprazole.**

sources.t: Cyriac JM, James E. Switch over from intravenous to oral therapy: a concise overview. J Pharmacol Pharmacother 2014;5:83-87

cases.title: The drugs that do NOT convert 1:1
cases.stem: A team asks for help converting several drugs before discharge.

steps.q: Furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily. Roughly what oral dose gives similar effect?

options.t: About 80 mg PO twice daily (IV to PO roughly 1:2)
options.why: Oral bioavailability is about 50% and varies; watch weight and urine output after the switch.
Usually gives less diuresis.

steps.q: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours. Oral equivalent?

options.why: Ciprofloxacin is about 70% absorbed, so the oral dose is higher.
There is no 400 mg tablet, and absorption is incomplete.

steps.q: Metoprolol tartrate 5 mg IV every 6 hours. Oral equivalent?

options.t: About 12.5 to 25 mg PO every 6 hours, or the same daily total as twice daily dosing
options.why: Oral metoprolol has large first pass loss; IV to PO is roughly 1:2.5. Titrate to heart rate and BP.
Far too low.

steps.q: Levothyroxine: how does IV compare with oral?

options.t: IV doses are lower, often about 50 to 75% of the oral dose, because oral absorption is incomplete
options.why: The label estimates relative oral bioavailability at about 48 to 74% and advises caution when converting.

options.t: IV dose is double the oral
options.why: Reversed.

cases.pearl: **Not 1:1: furosemide (x2 oral), cipro (higher oral), metoprolol (about x2.5 oral), levothyroxine (IV lower).**

cases.title: When NOT to switch
cases.stem: A patient with MRSA bacteremia has been afebrile for 24 hours. The team asks about oral linezolid on day 3.

steps.q: Which situations usually stay IV, at least early?

options.t: S. aureus bacteremia (especially early, before source control and clearance)
options.why: High mortality infection; oral step down is only considered in selected patients after clearance and ID input.
Needs high central nervous system concentrations.
The POET trial showed partial oral therapy was noninferior in selected stable patients after at least 10 days IV; this is an ID team decision.
A classic case for switching.

steps.q: Which patient factors block an oral switch?

options.t: Vomiting, ileus, severe diarrhea, or malabsorption
options.why: The drug has to be absorbed.

options.t: NPO for surgery or unable to swallow with no feeding tube
options.why: No route.

options.t: Unstable vital signs or worsening infection
options.why: Not ready.
That supports switching.

cases.pearl: **Stay IV: S. aureus bacteremia early, meningitis, endocarditis (team decision), a gut that does not work.**

sources.t: Iversen K, et al. Partial oral versus intravenous antibiotic treatment of endocarditis (POET). N Engl J Med 2019;380:415-424

cases.title: Chelation: the switch that fails
cases.stem: Switched from IV to oral ciprofloxacin. The home med list includes calcium carbonate, a multivitamin with iron and zinc, and magnesium oxide.

steps.q: What is the problem?

options.t: Calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron and zinc bind fluoroquinolones in the gut and can cut absorption dramatically
options.why: The IV dose had no such problem; the oral switch creates the interaction.
Chelation is one of the most common reasons oral antibiotics fail.

steps.q: What do you recommend?

options.t: Give ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after the minerals (per label), or hold the supplements during the course
options.why: Spacing or holding fixes it.
Raises toxicity without reliably fixing the binding.

steps.q: Which other oral antibiotics have the same chelation problem?

options.why: Same mechanism.
Not meaningfully affected.

cases.pearl: **Quinolones and tetracyclines + Ca, Mg, Al, Fe, Zn = no absorption. Space them.**

sources.t: DailyMed prescribing information for each drug named (Clinical Pharmacology and Drug Interactions sections)

cases.title: Feeding tube conversions
cases.setting: ICU · new NG tube with continuous feeds
cases.stem: A patient on continuous tube feeds needs phenytoin and levothyroxine switched from IV to the tube.

steps.q: What is the issue with phenytoin suspension and tube feeds?

options.t: Tube feeds can bind phenytoin and lower levels a lot; many protocols hold feeds 1 to 2 hours before and after each dose and monitor levels closely
options.why: Check a level after the switch and adjust.
This interaction is well known.

steps.q: Phenytoin capsules versus suspension: why can the dose change?

options.t: Extended capsules are phenytoin sodium (92% phenytoin); suspension and chewable tablets are phenytoin acid (100%)
options.why: Switching forms changes how much phenytoin the patient gets; small differences matter with its nonlinear kinetics.
Salt form matters for phenytoin.

steps.q: Which products should NOT be crushed for the tube?

options.t: Extended release and enteric coated tablets
options.why: Check the ISMP Do Not Crush list and switch to an immediate release or liquid form.
These can be crushed; give apart from feeds per protocol.

cases.pearl: **Tube feeds: phenytoin and feeds do not mix, salt forms differ, never crush ER or EC.**

cases.title: Linezolid switch, interaction check
cases.stem: Switching IV linezolid 600 mg every 12 hours to oral. Home meds include sertraline.

steps.q: What dose orally?

options.why: Linezolid is about 100% absorbed.
No increase needed.

steps.q: What interaction do you check?

options.t: Serotonin syndrome risk: linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor, and sertraline is serotonergic
options.why: Talk with the team about the risk, monitoring, or alternatives. The same applies to IV linezolid; the switch is a good moment to catch it.
Linezolid plus SSRIs is a classic interaction.

steps.q: What lab do you watch on longer courses?

options.t: Platelets and blood counts (myelosuppression, usually after about 2 weeks)
options.why: Also watch for lactic acidosis and neuropathy with long use.
Not the main concern.

cases.pearl: **Linezolid 1:1, but check for SSRIs and watch platelets.**

cases.title: Doing the IV to PO round
cases.stem: You run the daily IV to PO report for your units.

steps.q: How do you make the switch happen?

options.t: Use St. Mary's automatic conversion policy when the drug and patient qualify, and document the change
options.why: Many hospitals let pharmacists switch qualifying drugs per protocol.

options.t: For drugs outside the protocol, recommend the switch to the prescriber with the criteria met and the exact oral dose
options.why: Make it easy to say yes.

options.t: Switch everything without checking the patient
options.why: Each patient must meet the criteria.

cases.call: "Dr. ___, your patient in 412 is afebrile 48 hours, eating, and on IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours. Oral metronidazole is nearly 100% absorbed. May I change it to 500 mg PO every 8 hours?"
cases.pearl: **Run the report daily. Protocol where allowed, a clear recommendation everywhere else.**
